name: Tarsal strip procedure

lead: The tarsal strip is an eyelid operation that shortens and re-anchors the outer end of a loose lower lid to the bone of the outer eye socket. People look to it for a tighter, more youthful lower lid and less visible white below the iris (scleral show).

It was described in 1979 for lids that sag, turn outward (ectropion) or turn inward (entropion). Published studies are case series, retrospective reviews and a few randomised trials, mostly on functional eyelid problems and complications after lower blepharoplasty rather than purely cosmetic goals.

paras: Surgeons describe the problem as laxity of the lateral canthal tendon. A strip of tarsal plate at the outer lid is freed and fixed to the periosteum of the lateral orbital rim, tightening the lid against the eye. Results show once swelling settles, and the operation is sometimes combined with other eyelid surgery.

Lower-lid surgery carries a risk of lid retraction, scleral show and ectropion, which is why tarsal strip and similar techniques are also used to prevent and treat these problems. Outcomes depend on how lax the lid is beforehand and on surgeon technique.

chain: Lower lid anchored to orbital rim
angle.text: The tarsal strip tightens a lax lower eyelid by anchoring it to the outer orbital rim, reducing sagging and visible white below the iris for a tighter, more youthful lid. The result is visible after healing. It is an established oculoplastic operation studied mainly for lid function.

lead: The tarsal strip procedure, or lateral tarsal strip, is an oculoplastic operation that tightens a lax lower eyelid by anchoring the outer end of the lid to the lateral orbital rim. It was published in 1979 as a technique for paralytic or senile upper and lower lid laxity, lateral canthal tendon laxity or malposition, and for scarring-related lid shortening problems after earlier lid-tightening surgery.[1]

Its main medical uses are the correction of ectropion (outward-turning lid) and involutional entropion (inward-turning lid), and the prevention or treatment of lower lid malposition after lower-lid blepharoplasty.[2][3][4] In looksmaxxing communities it is mentioned as a hard-maxxing option for a sagging lower lid and visible sclera beneath the iris.

The published literature consists mainly of case series, retrospective reviews and a few randomised trials in functional eyelid problems. No studies were found that evaluate the procedure specifically for cosmetic eye-shape goals in otherwise normal lids.

paras: The technique addresses horizontal laxity of the lower lid, which its authors identified as the primary problem in most cases of senile or paralytic lid malposition. The tarsal plate at the lateral end of the lid is prepared as a strip and secured to the periosteum inside the outer orbital rim, shortening and tightening the lid.[1]

Later authors described an 'enhanced' version for patients with lid malposition but little loose skin, and in some cases a shortage of skin, in whom a standard tarsal strip alone was considered less suitable.[5]

Combined with everting sutures or fornix sutures, the tarsal strip has been used for involutional entropion; a retrospective study of 119 patients at Bascom Palmer Eye Institute evaluated long-term results of this combination.[3] A randomised controlled trial compared everting sutures alone with everting sutures plus a lateral tarsal strip in involutional entropion.[4]
Other reports describe it alongside Quickert sutures for entropion,[6] and with hard-palate grafts for lid retraction after blepharoplasty.[7]

Ectropion and scleral show are described as the most common complications of lower-lid blepharoplasty. A 1990 review proposed adding a wedge tarsectomy or tarsal strip to blepharoplasty in predisposed patients as a preventive measure and discussed conservative massage as first-line treatment of established postoperative ectropion.[2]
A 2015 retrospective review of lateral canthoplasty techniques for existing or potential lower-lid malposition identified seven key preoperative findings used to judge risk.[8]

The literature reviewed here treats lid malposition (ectropion, retraction, scleral show) as the principal problem that tightening procedures aim to prevent or correct, rather than as a risk specific to the tarsal strip itself.[2][8] Detailed complication rates for the tarsal strip are not summarised in the sources reviewed.

Published human studies are in functional eyelid conditions. They include a 1979 description of the technique,[1] a 1989 refinement,[5] retrospective series in involutional entropion,[3] a randomised controlled trial in involutional entropion,[4] and a retrospective review of lateral canthoplasty for lower-lid malposition.[8] A registered trial (NCT02893813, 22 participants) compared tarsal strip alone with tarsal strip plus punctoplasty for ectropion.[9] No studies were found that test the procedure for appearance alone in people without eyelid malposition.

timeline.event: The tarsal strip procedure is described in Archives of Ophthalmology.[1]
An 'enhanced tarsal strip' for patients without lax tissues is described.[5]
A review recommends considering tarsal strip or wedge tarsectomy to prevent ectropion after lower-lid blepharoplasty.[2]
A randomised trial compares everting sutures with and without a tarsal strip for entropion.[4]
A retrospective review identifies preoperative findings for lateral canthoplasty candidates.[8]
